science.title: Petrographic and geochemical characterization of Oba Ile granitoids and their implications for magma source and chemical weathering in southwestern Nigeria
science.description: The Oba-Ile area and environs in Akure, southwestern Nigeria, are underlain predominantly by granitoids of the Precambrian Nigerian Basement Complex. This study integrates field mapping, petrography, whole-rock major and selected trace element geochemistry, chemical weathering indices, and multivariate statistical analysis to constrain their geological evolution and petrogenesis. Major and selected trace elements were determined using Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometry (AAS). Field investigations identified a heterogeneous basement assemblage comprising migmatite gneiss, granite gneiss, porphyritic granite and fine-grained granite, with subordinate pegmatite, aplite, dolerite, and quartz to quartzofeldspathic veins. The granitoids comprise mainly quartz, feldspar, biotite, and hornblende, with minor zircon and pyroxene. SiO₂ contents range from 58.23 to 78.40 wt%, defining intermediate to felsic compositions. Decreases in Fe₂O₃, CaO, MgO, P₂O₅, and MnO with increasing SiO₂ indicate progressive magmatic differentiation dominated by fractional crystallization. The granitoids are predominantly calc-alkaline and metaluminous to peraluminous, suggesting heterogeneous crustal sources, substantial crustal involvement, and possible metasedimentary contributions, consistent with crustal reworking and felsic magmatism during convergent to post-collisional Pan-African tectonothermal evolution. Predominant N–S joints and NE–SW veins record post-emplacement brittle deformation and localized fluid movement. CIA values of 57.70–77.60 indicate slight to moderate chemical weathering, while PCA defines Co–Mn–Cr–Ni, Zn–Cu–Fe–Cd, and Zr–Pb associations, reflecting primary mineral partitioning, magmatic differentiation, and weathering modification rather than hydrothermal mineralization. Overall, the granitoids record multistage magmatic evolution, crustal reworking, structural modification, and tropical weathering. However, interpretation of trace-element behaviour is constrained by the use of acid-leachable AAS methods, particularly for refractory elements, and the absence of high-resolution whole-rock, isotopic, and mineral-chemical datasets. Consequently, the results provide a first-order petrogenetic framework, while future XRF, ICP-MS, and isotopic analyses are recommended to refine source, timing, and crustal evolution models.
